title: Polymorphism
summary: One interface, many forms. Learn how the same method call can behave differently depending on the object behind it.

blocks.markdown:
**Polymorphism** (Greek for "many forms") means one interface — a shared method name — can behave differently depending on the object that receives the call.

- Callers write code against a **common method name**, not a specific type.
- The actual behavior is decided by **which object** is behind the call.
- It comes in two flavors: chosen at **compile time** (overloading) or at **runtime** (overriding).
- Builds directly on [inheritance](inheritance) — a subtype's objects can stand in for their parent type.

blocks.subTitle: Two flavors
blocks.markdown:
The two kinds you'll meet, side by side.

| | Static | Dynamic |
|---|---|---|
| Decided | Compile time | Runtime |
| Mechanism | Overloading | Overriding |

Both let one method name cover several behaviors — just at different points in time.

**Compile-time (static) polymorphism** happens through **method overloading** — defining several methods with the **same name** but different parameters (count, type, or order).

- The compiler picks the right version by matching the **arguments** you pass, before the program ever runs.
- Same name, different **signature** — the method's name plus its parameter list.
- Common example: `area(radius)` for a circle and `area(width, height)` for a rectangle, both named `area`.

blocks.subTitle: Pseudocode: overloading
blocks.markdown:
```text
class Calculator:
    method add(a: int, b: int) -> int:
        return a + b

    method add(a: int, b: int, c: int) -> int:
        return a + b + c

    method add(a: float, b: float) -> float:
        return a + b

calc = new Calculator()
calc.add(2, 3)        // matches add(int, int)      -> 5
calc.add(2, 3, 4)     // matches add(int, int, int) -> 9
calc.add(2.5, 3.5)    // matches add(float, float)  -> 6.0
```

The compiler resolves each call to a specific `add` using the argument list alone — no object state is involved.

**Runtime (dynamic) polymorphism** happens through **method overriding** — a subclass redefines a method it inherited from its parent, keeping the **same name and signature**.

- Which version runs is decided while the program is **executing**, based on the object's **actual type**.
- Requires [inheritance](inheritance): the subclass must already have the method to override.
- Example: `Dog` and `Cat` both override `Animal.makeSound()` with their own version.

**Dynamic dispatch** is the mechanism that makes overriding work: at runtime, the call is routed to the method defined on the object's **actual (runtime) type**, not the type of the variable holding it.

- Methods eligible for this are often called **virtual methods** — the language keeps a lookup so each object type resolves to its own version.
- The variable's declared type only decides **what calls are allowed**; the object's real type decides **which body runs**.
- This indirection is what lets the same line of code produce different behavior for different objects.

blocks.sectionTitle: Upcasting and programming to an interface
blocks.markdown:
**Upcasting** is treating a subtype object as an instance of its parent type or interface — assigning a `Dog` to an `Animal`-typed variable.

- It's always safe: every `Dog` **is an** `Animal`, so nothing is lost by viewing it more generally.
- **Programming to an interface** means writing code against the parent type or interface, so it works with any subtype without change.
- This is what lets a single function accept `Animal` and correctly handle a `Dog`, `Cat`, or any future subtype.

The classic mix-up, cleared up.

| | Overloading | Overriding |
|---|---|---|
| Resolved | Compile time | Runtime |
| Signature | Must differ | Must match exactly |
| Relationship | Same class | Parent/subclass |

Overloading gives one class several versions of a name; overriding lets a subclass replace one it already has.

Polymorphism is what lets you **add new types without touching existing code**.

- Code written against a parent type (`Animal`, `Shape`) already works with any new subtype you add later.
- Adding a `Bird` subclass means writing `Bird`, not editing every function that loops over animals.
- This is the practical payoff behind [design-patterns-overview](design-patterns-overview) like Strategy and Visitor — they all lean on swapping behavior through one shared interface.

Common mistakes:

- **Confusing overloading with overriding.** Different parameter lists in the same class is overloading, not polymorphism in the runtime sense.
- **Changing the signature and calling it an override.** If the parameters don't match exactly, most languages treat it as a new overload, silently hiding the parent method instead of replacing it.
- **Downcasting to avoid overriding.** Checking the object's type and branching (`if dog... else if cat...`) defeats the point — let dynamic dispatch pick the behavior instead.

blocks.subTitle: Overloading vs overriding
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: What's the difference between overloading and overriding?**

**Overloading** is same name, different parameters, resolved at **compile time**, within one class. **Overriding** is same name and same signature, resolved at **runtime**, redefining a method a subclass inherited from its parent. Overloading adds variety; overriding replaces behavior.

blocks.subTitle: Dynamic dispatch
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: What is dynamic dispatch, and how does it work?**

It's the runtime mechanism that routes a method call to the version defined on the object's actual type, not the variable's declared type. The language keeps a per-type lookup for overridable (virtual) methods, so `animal.makeSound()` resolves to `Dog`'s version when `animal` actually holds a `Dog` — decided fresh at each call, not baked in at compile time.

blocks.subTitle: Compile-time vs runtime
blocks.markdown:
**Q: Compile-time vs runtime polymorphism — when is each decided?**

Compile-time polymorphism (overloading) is resolved while the code is being compiled, purely from the arguments' types and count. Runtime polymorphism (overriding) is resolved while the program runs, based on the object actually sitting behind the reference at that moment.

blocks.subTitle: Extensibility payoff
blocks.markdown:
**Q: How does polymorphism make a design more extensible?**

Code written against a parent type or interface keeps working when you add new subtypes, because the call site never mentions the concrete type. Adding a new shape or payment method means writing a new class that fits the existing interface — no existing function that loops over the parent type needs to change.

blocks.subTitle: Programming to an interface
blocks.markdown:
**Q: What does "programming to an interface, not an implementation" mean?**

Write code that depends only on the methods a parent type or interface promises, never on a specific subclass. A variable declared as `Animal` can hold any subtype; the calling code stays correct and unchanged no matter which concrete class is passed in.

blocks.subTitle: Upcasting safety
blocks.markdown:
**Q: Why is upcasting always safe, but downcasting isn't?**

Upcasting (subtype to parent type) is safe because every subtype instance genuinely satisfies the parent's contract — a `Dog` really is an `Animal`. Downcasting (parent type back to a specific subtype) assumes something that isn't guaranteed — the object behind an `Animal` reference might be a `Cat`, not the `Dog` you're casting to — so it can fail at runtime.
